name: 2 Esdras
sourceNote:
Translated from the Latin text of 4 Esdras as printed in the appendix to the Clementine Vulgate (1592), with the “missing fragment” of chapter 7 (7:36–105) translated from the Latin text published by Robert L. Bensly, The Missing Fragment of the Latin Translation of the Fourth Book of Ezra (Cambridge, 1875). Where the Latin is plainly corrupt or has lost words, the sense of the oriental versions (Syriac, Ethiopic, and others) is sometimes followed; these are cited only as reported in the scholarly literature, not from a fresh collation, and every such place is marked in the notes.

The name. The book called 2 Esdras in the English Apocrypha (and in the King James Version) is printed as 4 Esdras in the appendix to the Latin Vulgate, where 1 and 2 Esdras are Ezra and Nehemiah and 3 Esdras is the book called 1 Esdras in English. It is not in the Septuagint. Esdras is the Greek and Latin form of the name Ezra (“help”).

Contents. The book is made of three originally separate works. Chapters 3–14 (often called 4 Ezra) are a Jewish apocalypse written about AD 100, some thirty years after the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, though set in Babylon thirty years after the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC. In seven visions, Ezra (here also called Salathiel, 3:1) wrestles with the angel Uriel over why God has let Zion fall and why so few will be saved, and is then shown the heavenly Zion (ch. 10), the eagle of Rome and the lion who is the Messiah (chs. 11–12), the man from the sea (ch. 13), and his own restoration of the scriptures (ch. 14). It was written in Hebrew or Aramaic, translated into Greek, and from the Greek into Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, Armenian, Georgian, Arabic, and other languages; the Semitic original and nearly all of the Greek are lost. Chapters 1–2 (often called 5 Ezra) are a Christian addition, probably of the 2nd or 3rd century AD, in which God rejects Israel for a new people; chapters 15–16 (often called 6 Ezra) are another Christian addition, reportedly of the 3rd century, prophesying woe on Babylon, Asia, Egypt, and Syria and encouraging believers under persecution. A small Greek fragment of 15:57–59 reportedly survives on papyrus. Chapters 1–2 and 15–16 are found only in Latin.

The missing fragment. In the Clementine Vulgate and the King James Version, chapter 7 passes directly from verse 35 to the verse that is 7:106 here, because a leaf had been cut from the ninth-century Codex Sangermanensis, from which most Latin copies descend. Bensly published the lost seventy verses from a ninth-century manuscript at Amiens in 1875, and they have been included in English versions since the Revised Version Apocrypha (1895). As a result KJV 7:36–70 is 7:106–140 here (see the notes at 7:35, 7:105, and 7:106).

Versification. The chapter and verse numbering follows that of most modern English versions (16 chapters, 944 verses). Where the Clementine Latin divides verses differently (for example at 5:55–56, 10:59–60, and 14:47–48, and in chapter 7), the difference is noted. A few half-sentences that the Latin places at the end of one verse are moved to the beginning of the next, as noted.

Status. 2 Esdras is part of the Apocrypha in Protestant Bibles; in Roman Catholic Bibles it appears (as 4 Esdras) only in the appendix to the Vulgate, together with 3 Esdras and the Prayer of Manasseh. It is not in the canon of the Greek Orthodox Church; chapters 3–14 are reportedly canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and the book is reportedly printed in Slavonic and Armenian Bibles. Latin Dominus is translated “Lord,” Altissimus “the Most High,” Fortis “the Mighty One,” and the address dominator Domine “Lord and Master.”

verses.text: The second book of the prophet Ezra,{b} the son of Sareus, the son of Azareus, the son of Helcias, the son of Sadanias, the son of Sadoc, the son of Achitob,

the son of Achias, the son of Phinees, the son of Heli, the son of Amerias, the son of Asiel, the son of Marimoth, the son of Arna, the son of Ozias, the son of Borith, the son of Abiseus, the son of Phinees, the son of Eleazar,
son of Aaron, of the tribe of Levi, who was a captive in the land of the Medes in the reign of Artaxerxes king of the Persians.{c}
And this word from the Lord{d} came to me:
“Go and declare to my people their crimes, and to their children the wrongs they have committed against me, so that they may tell their children’s children;
for the sins of their parents have grown great in them; they have forgotten me and offered sacrifice to foreign gods.
Was it not I who brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery? Yet they have provoked me to anger and scorned my counsels.
But as for you, pull out the hair of your head{e} and hurl all evils upon them, for they have not obeyed my law; they are an undisciplined people.
How long shall I bear with them, on whom I have bestowed such great benefits?
On their account I overturned many kings; Pharaoh, together with his servants and his whole host, I struck down.
I destroyed all the nations before them; and in the east I scattered the peoples of two provinces, Tyre and Sidon,{f} and I killed all their enemies.
“But you, speak to them and say, ‘Thus says the Lord:
Surely it was I who brought you through the sea, and made for you walled highways where there had been none.{g} I gave you Moses as your leader and Aaron as your priest;
I provided you light from a pillar of fire, and did great wonders among you. Yet you have forgotten me, says the Lord.
“‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: The quail was a sign to you; I gave you a camp for your protection, and there you grumbled.
You did not exult in my name at the destruction of your enemies, but even to this day you still grumble.
What has become of the kindnesses I showed you? In the desert, when hunger came on you, did you not cry aloud to me
saying, “Why have you brought us into this wilderness to kill us? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness”?
I pitied your groaning and gave you manna for food; you ate the bread of angels.
When thirst came on you, was it not I who cut open the rock, and waters ran out until you had your fill? Against the burning heat I sheltered you with leaves from the trees.{h}
I divided fertile lands among you; I drove out the Canaanites and the Perizzites and the Philistines before you. What more shall I do for you? says the Lord.
“‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: When you were in the wilderness at the river of the Amorites,{i} thirsty and blaspheming my name,
I sent no fire on you in return for your blasphemies, but cast a piece of wood into the water and turned the river sweet.
What shall I do to you, Jacob? You would not obey, Judah. I will turn to other nations and give them my name, so that they may keep my statutes.
Because you have forsaken me, I also will forsake you. When you ask me for mercy, I will show you none.
When you call upon me, I will not listen to you; for you have defiled your hands with blood, and your feet are swift to commit murder.
Yet it is not I that you have abandoned, but your own selves, says the Lord.
“‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: Have I not pleaded with you as a father pleads with his sons, or a mother with her daughters, or a nurse with her little ones,
that you should be my people and I your God, that you should be my children and I your father?
I gathered you as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.{j} But now, what shall I do to you? I will cast you out from my presence.
When you bring me offerings, I will turn my face from you; for I have rejected your feast days and new moons and circumcisions.
I sent you my servants the prophets, and you took them and killed them and mutilated their bodies; I will require their blood, says the Lord.
“‘This is what the Lord Almighty says: Your house is left a desert. I will toss you away as the wind tosses stubble;
and your children will have no offspring, because they have neglected my commandment and done what is evil in my sight.
I will hand over your houses to a people that is coming, who will believe though they have not heard me; to whom I have shown no signs, yet they will do what I have commanded.
They have not seen the prophets, yet they will call to mind the wrongs of those before them.{k}
I call to witness the gratitude of the people that is coming, whose little ones leap for joy; they do not see me with bodily eyes, yet in spirit they believe what I have said.
“‘And now, brother,{l} behold the glory, and look upon the people that comes from the sunrise;
I will grant them for guides Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah,
Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, whom men also call the angel of the Lord.’ ”{m}

notes.text: Chapters 1–2 are a later Christian addition to the book, often called 5 Ezra (Fifth Ezra); they are written as a prophecy of Ezra rejecting Israel in favor of a people “coming from the east” and are generally dated to the 2nd or 3rd century AD. They are preserved only in Latin, in two forms (a “French” and a “Spanish” family of manuscripts, as reported); this translation follows the Clementine Vulgate text, with significant differences noted. See the introduction to the book.

Ezra means “help.” The genealogy follows Ezra 7:1–5 with additions (Ahijah, Eli, Aziel, Arna, Borith; compare 1 Chronicles 6:4–14). Seraiah means “Yahweh contends”; Hilkiah, “Yahweh is my portion”; Zadok, “righteous”; Phinehas is an Egyptian name, “the Nubian”; Eleazar means “God has helped.” The names are given here in their Latin forms: Sareus is Seraiah, Azareus Azariah, Helcias Hilkiah, Sadanias perhaps Shallum, Sadoc Zadok, Achitob Ahitub, Achias Ahijah, Phinees Phinehas, Heli Eli, Amerias Amariah, Marimoth Meraioth, Ozias Uzzi, and Abiseus Abishua.
Artaxerxes (Persian Artakhshassa) was the king under whom Ezra came to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:1). The statement that Ezra was a captive in Media is found only here.
Latin Dominus, “Lord.” In this book, which survives from the Latin, “Lord” renders Dominus throughout, and “the Lord Almighty” renders Dominus omnipotens.
A sign of grief and anger; compare Ezra 9:3.
Latin “the peoples of two provinces, Tyre and Sidon”; the text is uncertain, and some manuscripts reportedly lack the names.
Latin “I showed you streets (or broad ways) fortified from the beginning”; compare Exodus 14:22, where the waters were a wall on either side.
An addition to the Exodus story, not found in the Hebrew Bible; compare Wisdom 19:7 and the shade of Psalm 105:39 (Septuagint 104:39).
Latin “in the river of the Amorites”; the story is that of Marah (Exodus 15:22–25), and the location is uncertain.
Compare Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34; chapters 1–2 contain many echoes of the New Testament.
Latin “and they will remember their iniquities,” that is, perhaps, the new people will recall the sins of Israel; the sense is debated, and other manuscripts reportedly read differently.
Latin frater, “brother,” in the Clementine text; other manuscripts reportedly have pater, “father,” which fits 2:5. The Lord addresses Ezra. Latin “see what glory,” perhaps “see with pride.”

Malachi means “my messenger” (Malachi 3:1); the Latin adds that he “is also called the angel of the Lord,” reflecting a tradition, found also in the Targum, that the prophet was an angel or identifying him with Ezra himself. The twelve Minor Prophets are listed in the order of the Septuagint for the first six.

chapters.title: The Second Book of Ezra the Prophet{a}

verses.text: This is what the Lord says: “I led this people out of bondage, and gave them commands by my servants the prophets; they refused to hear them and set my counsels at nothing.
The mother who bore them{a} says to them, ‘Go, my children, for I am a widow and forsaken.
I brought you up with gladness, and I have lost you with mourning and sorrow, because you have sinned before the Lord your God and done what is evil in his sight.
But now what can I do for you? I am a widow and forsaken. Go, my children, and ask the Lord for mercy.’
But you, father,{b} I summon to bear witness, along with the children’s mother, that they refused to keep my covenant,
that you may bring confusion upon them, and give their mother up to plunder, so that they may have no offspring.
Scatter their names among the nations; wipe them out from the earth, for they have treated my sacred pledge with contempt.{c}
“Woe to you, Assyria,{d} who hide the unrighteous in your midst! Wicked nation, remember what I did to Sodom and Gomorrah,
whose land lies in lumps of pitch and heaps of ashes. So I will make those who have not listened to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
This is what the Lord says to Ezra: “Announce to my people that the kingdom of Jerusalem, which I meant for Israel, I will give to them.
Their glory I will take for myself, and to these I will give the everlasting tents I had made ready for the others.
They will have the tree of life for fragrant perfume, and they will neither toil nor grow weary.
Go, and you will receive; pray that the days may be few for you, that they may be shortened.{e} The kingdom is already prepared for you; watch!
Call heaven and earth to witness; for I have broken evil in pieces and created good, for I live, says the Lord.
“Mother, embrace your children; bring them up with gladness. Make their feet firm like a dove’s, for I have chosen you, says the Lord.
And I will raise the dead from their places, and bring them out of their tombs, for I have recognized my name in them.{f}
Do not be afraid, mother of the children, for I have chosen you, says the Lord.
To help you I will send my servants Isaiah and Jeremiah. By their counsel I have hallowed and made ready for you twelve trees heavy with fruits of many kinds,
and as many springs flowing with milk and honey, and seven mighty mountains on which roses and lilies grow;{g} by these I will fill your children with joy.
Do justice for the widow, secure justice for the ward, give to the needy, protect the orphan, clothe the naked,
care for the broken and the weak, do not mock the lame, protect the maimed, and let the blind come into the sight of my splendor.
Guard the old and the young within your walls.
Wherever you find the dead, sign them and commit them to the tomb,{h} and I will give you the first seat in my resurrection.
Stop, my people, and take your rest, for your rest is on its way.
Good nurse, nourish your children; make their feet firm.
As for the servants whom I have given you, not one of them shall perish, for I will require them from among your number.
Do not be weary; for when the day of distress and anguish comes, others will weep and be sorrowful, but you will be cheerful and have plenty.
The nations will envy you, but they will be able to do nothing against you, says the Lord.
My hands will cover you, so that your children may not see Gehenna.{i}
Rejoice, mother, with your children, for I will deliver you, says the Lord.
Remember your children who sleep, for I will bring them out of the hiding places of the earth{j} and show mercy to them; for I am merciful, says the Lord Almighty.
Embrace your children until I come, and proclaim mercy to them;{k} for my springs overflow, and my grace will not fail.”
I, Ezra, received a command from the Lord on Mount Horeb{l} to go to Israel; but when I came to them, they rejected me and refused the Lord’s commandment.
Therefore I say to you, O nations that hear and understand, “Await your shepherd; he will give you everlasting rest, for he who will come at the end of the age is close at hand.
Be ready for the rewards of the kingdom, for everlasting light will shine upon you for evermore.
Escape from the shadow of this world, and take hold of the delight of your glory. I openly bear witness to my Savior.{m}
Receive what has been entrusted to you and be glad, giving thanks to him who has called you to the heavenly kingdoms.
Rise up and stand, and see the number of those who have been sealed{n} at the feast of the Lord.
They who have passed over out of the world’s shadow have been given shining robes by the Lord.
Take again your full number, O Zion, and close the list of those of yours who are clothed in white,{o} who have fulfilled the law of the Lord.
The number of your children whom you desired is full; implore the authority of the Lord that your people, who have been called from the beginning, may be made holy.”
I, Ezra, saw upon Mount Zion a vast throng, more than I could count, and with songs they were all praising the Lord.
Among them stood a youth of lofty stature, higher than all the rest, who set crowns upon the head of each one, and he was lifted up all the more. And I was held fast in wonder.
Then I asked the angel, “Who are these, my lord?”
He replied, “These have laid aside the garment of mortality and taken on the garment of immortality, and they have confessed God’s name. Now they receive their crowns and their palms.”
And I asked the angel, “And that youth who sets the crowns on them and gives the palms into their hands, who is he?”
He replied, “It is the Son of God, whom they confessed in this world.” Then I began to extol those who had stood firm and brave for the Lord’s name.
Then the angel said to me, “Go, tell my people what kind of wonders of the Lord God you have seen, and how great they are.”

notes.text: The mother is Jerusalem or Zion (compare Baruch 4:9–23; Isaiah 54:1); later in the chapter (2:15–17) the mother is the church of the new people.
Latin pater, “father,” that is, Ezra, or perhaps God; the text is uncertain.
Latin sacramentum, “sacred pledge,” a word used of covenant and oath.
The Latin has Assur, the old name of Assyria, here probably a symbol for Rome or for a hostile power; compare 15:28–33.
Latin “ask for yourselves few days, that they may linger,” an obscure phrase; the sense may be that the days before the end should be shortened (compare Matthew 24:22).
Latin “for I have known my name in Israel”; the Clementine text, followed here, reads “in Israel,” which seems contrary to the context; other manuscripts reportedly read differently.
The twelve trees, springs of milk and honey, and seven mountains recall Revelation 22:2 and the paradise traditions of 1 Enoch 24–25; compare also 2 Esdras 2:12.
Latin signans, “marking with a sign,” perhaps the sign of the cross in burial; compare Tobit 1:17–18 on burying the dead.
Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:31–32), became a name for the place of fiery punishment of the wicked; compare 7:36.
Latin “from the sides (or hidden recesses) of the earth.”
Latin “and that I may show them mercy.”
Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:1; Deuteronomy 5:2). The writer presents Ezra as a second Moses (compare 14:3–4).
Latin “I testify openly to my Savior,” a plainly Christian phrase; Ezra speaks as a herald of Christ.
Compare Revelation 7:3–4, the sealing of the servants of God.
Latin candidatos, “those clothed in white”; compare Revelation 3:4–5; 7:9, 13–14.

verses.text: In the thirtieth year{a} after the ruin of the city{b} I was in Babylon. I lay troubled upon my bed, and my thoughts rose up over my heart,
for I had seen Zion forsaken, and the plenty of those who dwelt in Babylon.
My spirit was sorely shaken, and I began to address the Most High{c} with fearful words.
I said, “Lord and Master, at the beginning, when you planted the earth, you spoke, you alone, and gave command to the dust,{d}
and it yielded you Adam, a body without life. Yet he too was something your hands had shaped; you blew into him a spirit of life, and he came alive before you.
You brought him into the garden your right hand had planted before ever the earth came forth.{e}
To him you gave charge to love your way, but he went beyond it; and at once you laid death upon him and upon his generations. From him sprang nations and tribes, peoples and kindreds beyond count.
Each nation went its own willful road; they did outrageous things before you and scorned your precepts.
Again, in due season, you sent a deluge over those who peopled the world, and wiped them out.
And the same lot fell on each: as death fell to Adam, so the deluge to these.
Yet one among them you spared, Noah{f} and his house, and from him came all the just.
Then, when earth’s inhabitants began to increase and had multiplied sons and peoples and many nations, they set about wickedness again, worse than the first.
And while they were doing evil before you, you picked out one man among them for yourself; Abraham{g} was his name.
Him you loved, and to him only you disclosed your will.
You set up an eternal covenant with him and told him you would never abandon his seed. You granted him Isaac, and to Isaac you granted Jacob and Esau.
Jacob you kept apart for yourself; Esau you put away. And Jacob grew into a vast throng.
When you brought his seed up out of Egypt, you led them to Mount Sinai.
You bowed the heavens and shook{h} the earth; you moved the globe and set the abysses trembling and threw the world into confusion.
Through four gates your glory went, fire and earthquake, wind and frost,{i} that you might give a law to Jacob’s seed, and diligent teaching to the line of Israel.
Still you did not remove the wicked heart from them, so that your law could yield its fruit in them.
For the first Adam, carrying a wicked heart, broke your command and was overpowered, and so too all born from him.
So the weakness stayed on; the law was in the people’s heart, but with the root’s malice in it,{j} and the good went away while the wicked remained.
Times went by, the years ran out, and you raised up a servant for yourself called David.
You bade him build a city to your name and offer you frankincense and offerings in it.
For many years this was so. Then the city’s people fell into sin,
in all things acting just as Adam and all his generations acted, for they too bore the wicked heart.
So you handed your city over into your enemies’ hands.
“Then I said in my heart, ‘Do Babylon’s people act any better? Is that why she lords it over Zion?’{k}
For when I arrived here I beheld ungodliness past counting; these thirty years my soul has looked on a multitude of wrongdoers, and my heart sank within me.
I saw how you put up with their sinning, how you spare the godless, while your own people you have destroyed and your foes you have kept safe; and you have not made known{l}
to anyone how your way is to be grasped.{m} Is Babylon’s conduct better than Zion’s?
Has some other nation known you, apart from Israel? Or which tribes have trusted your covenants as Jacob has?
Yet no wage of theirs has come to light, and their toil has yielded nothing. I have traveled widely among the nations and seen them thriving, and they give no thought to your commands.
So now put our wrongs and the wrongs of the world’s dwellers on the scales, and it will become plain which side the balance tips toward.{n}
When did the dwellers on earth ever fail to sin before you? What nation has observed your commands like this?
Men you may find, one by one and named, who have kept your commands; nations you will not find.”

notes.text: Chapters 3–14 are the original Jewish apocalypse called 4 Ezra, written about AD 100 after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70), in Hebrew or Aramaic; the original and the Greek translation are lost, and the book survives in Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, and other versions. It consists of seven visions or episodes (3:1–5:20; 5:21–6:34; 6:35–9:25; 9:26–10:59; 11:1–12:51; 13:1–58; 14:1–48).

The thirtieth year after the destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC would be about 557 BC, a symbolic date that also points to about AD 100, thirty years after the Romans destroyed the city. The Clementine Latin begins here; other Latin manuscripts and the oriental versions reportedly begin, “I, Salathiel, who am also called Ezra,” identifying the seer with Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:17; Ezra 3:2).
Latin Altissimus, “the Most High,” the commonest name for God in this book.
Latin “you commanded the people,” evidently a corruption; the sense required is “the dust,” from which Adam was made, as the Syriac reportedly reads.
Latin “before the earth came forward”; the garden was believed to have been created before the world (compare 6:2–6; Genesis 2:8, where the Hebrew miqqedem can mean “from of old”).
Noah means “rest.”
Abraham means “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17:5).
Latin statuisti, “you set (the earth) fast”; the Syriac reportedly reads “shook,” which suits the context.
Compare Exodus 19:16–18 and Psalm 68:8. The “four gates” are perhaps four heavenly regions through which the glory of God passed to Sinai.
Latin “with the malignity of the root”; the “evil heart” (Latin cor malignum) corresponds to the rabbinic notion of the evil inclination (yetzer ha-ra).
Babylon is a cipher for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8 and 1 Peter 5:13.
The Latin of verses 30–31 is broken; it reads literally “and you did not indicate. I do not remember at all how this way should be forsaken.” The rendering follows the general sense.
See the previous note.
Latin “and your name will not be found except in Israel,” which does not fit the sense; the rendering follows the reading reported in the oriental versions (“which way the scale inclines”).

verses.text: The angel sent to me, named Uriel,{a} replied to me
and said, “In this world your heart has quite overreached itself. Do you mean to grasp the Most High’s way?”
“Yes, my lord,” I said. He replied, “Three ways I have been sent to show you, and three likenesses to put before you.
Explain one of these to me, and I in turn will point out the way you yearn to see and teach you the origin of the wicked heart.”
“Speak on, my lord,” I said. He said to me, “Go and weigh out for me the heaviness of fire; or take the measure for me of a gust of wind; or summon back for me a day already gone.”
I replied, “What human born could do such things, that you put such questions to me?”

He said to me, “Suppose I had questioned you thus: ‘How many dwellings lie in the sea’s heart? How many springs at the head of the abyss? How many channels above the firmament? Where are the ways out of paradise?’
You might perhaps have told me, ‘Into the abyss I have not gone down, nor yet into the underworld,{b} and up to heaven I never climbed.’
But I have questioned you only on fire and wind and day, which you have lived through and cannot be parted from, and you have given me no reply concerning them.”
Then he told me, “What is yours and has grown up along with you, you cannot know;
so how should your vessel{c} have room for the Most High’s way? How can a man worn away by a decaying world understand what does not decay?”{d} Hearing this, I fell face down{e}
and told him, “Better for us never to have been than to come and live amid godlessness and suffer without knowing the reason.”
He replied, “Once I went out to a wood of trees on the plain, and they took counsel together.
‘Come,’ they said, ‘let us march and wage war on the sea, to drive it back before us and gain more woodland for ourselves.’
The sea’s billows took counsel the same way: ‘Come,’ they said, ‘let us go up and defeat the plain’s woodland, and so there too win fresh country for ourselves.’
The wood’s scheme was in vain; fire came and devoured it.
So too the billows’ scheme; the sand rose against them and barred their way.
Had you been set to judge them, which would you have begun to acquit, and which to convict?”
I replied, “Both of them schemed foolishly. The dry ground has been allotted to the wood, and to the sea a place for carrying its billows.”
He replied, “Your verdict is a good one. Then why not give the same verdict upon yourself?
As dry ground belongs to the wood and the sea to its billows, so earth’s dwellers can grasp only what pertains to earth, and he who dwells above the heavens what lies at the heights of heaven.”{f}
I replied, “I beg you, lord, why{g} was the faculty of understanding granted me?

It was not about things on high that I meant to ask, but about what passes by us daily: why Israel has been made a laughingstock to the nations; why the people you loved has been surrendered to godless tribes; why our fathers’ law has been wiped out, and the written covenants are nowhere to be found.
We go out of the world as locusts do; our life is bewilderment and dread,{h} and we do not deserve to receive mercy.
Then what will he do for the sake of his name, called over us? Those are my questions.”
He replied, “If you live, you will see; and if you search far, many times you will wonder;{i} for the world is rushing quickly toward its passing.
It cannot contain what is pledged to the just for the times to come, since this world is crammed with wrong and weakness.
As to what you ask: evil has indeed been sown, yet its overthrow is still to come.
Unless, then, the sown crop is cut down, and the ground where evil was planted vanishes, the place planted with good cannot arrive.
A seed of wicked grain was planted in Adam’s heart at the start; what a crop of godlessness it has raised to this day, and will raise until the threshing floor arrives!
Reckon up for yourself what a yield of godlessness one seed of wicked grain has brought forth.
When ears beyond counting are reaped, what a vast threshing floor will they make!”
I replied, “How, and when, will this happen? Why are our years short and wretched?”
He replied, “Do not outrun the Most High. Your eagerness is on your own account,{j} but the One on high hastens for the sake of multitudes.
Did not the souls of the just, in their storehouses, raise these very questions: ‘For how long shall we wait in this way?{k} When comes the fruit of the threshing floor, our wage?’
To them Jeremiel{l} the archangel made answer: ‘When the full count of ones such as you is reached;{m} for he has weighed the world on scales,
the seasons he has measured with a measure and counted with a count, and he will neither stir nor rouse them until the measure foretold is filled.’ ”
I replied, “Lord and Master, yet all of us too are brimming with godlessness.
Perhaps it is our doing that the just are kept from their threshing floor, because of the sins of earth’s dwellers.”
He replied, “Go, inquire of a woman with child, when she has finished her ninth month, whether her womb is still able to hold the infant back inside her.”
“It is not able, lord,” I said. He told me, “In the underworld the souls’ storehouses resemble a womb.
Just as one giving birth presses on to be free of the pains of labor, so these press on to give up what was committed to them.
Then what you long to see will be disclosed to you from the start.”
I replied, “If I have found grace in your eyes, if it can be, and if I am worthy,
disclose this to me: is more yet to come than what is over, or have greater things gone by than what lies ahead?
The past I know; what lies ahead I cannot tell.”
He told me, “Take your stand on the right, and I will give you the interpretation of a likeness.”
I stood and watched, and there before me a burning oven went past; when the blaze had gone, I watched, and look, smoke was left over.
Next a cloud brimming with water went past me and let loose a great downpour with force; and once the force of the rain was spent, raindrops were left in it.
He told me, “Think it over: as the rain exceeded the drops and the fire the smoke, so the measure already gone by far exceeded the rest. Yet the drops and the smoke were left.”
Then I prayed: “Will I be alive, do you think, until that time? Or what will happen in that time?”
He replied, “About the signs you inquire of, I can tell you a portion. But about your own life I was not sent to speak to you; indeed I do not know.

notes.text: Uriel means “God is my light.” In 1 Enoch 20:2 he is one of the archangels, set over the world and over Tartarus.
Latin infernum, the world of the dead (Hebrew Sheol).
That is, the mind, as the container of understanding (compare 2 Corinthians 4:7).
Latin “understand the corruption evident in my face,” an obscure phrase; the rendering follows the sense of the oriental versions as reported (“the incorruptible”).
The words “When I heard this, I fell on my face” are not in the Clementine Latin; they are reportedly found in the Syriac and Ethiopic and are supplied here for the sense.
Compare John 3:12, 31.
Latin “that I may be given the sense of understanding,” here with a question as in the oriental versions, as reported.
Latin stupor et pavor, “astonishment and fear”; other witnesses reportedly read “a vapor,” in line with James 4:14. The text is uncertain.
Latin “If you search much, you will often marvel”; the rendering combines the Latin with the fuller reading reported in the oriental versions.
Latin “For you hasten vainly to be above him, for your excess is great.” The rendering follows the clearer sense reported in the oriental versions.
Latin “How long do I hope thus?”
Jeremiel (Hebrew perhaps Jerahmeel, “God has mercy,” or Ramiel, “God is exalted”) is named as an archangel set over the risen souls in 1 Enoch 20:8 (Remiel, in the Greek).
Latin “When the number of seeds in you is completed.” Compare Revelation 6:9–11, where the souls under the altar are told to wait until the number of their fellow servants is complete.

verses.text: “But as to the signs: look, days are coming when earth’s dwellers will be seized with great dismay,{a} and the way of truth will be hidden away, and the land will be barren of faith.
Wrong will increase beyond what you now see yourself, and beyond what you heard of long ago.
And the country you now see ruling will be trackless, and men will see it laid waste.{b}
Should the Most High grant you life, you will see it after the third trumpet;{c} then all at once the sun will shine out again by night, and the moon three times by day.
Blood will drip out of wood, and stone will give forth its voice; peoples will be in an uproar,
and one will reign whom earth’s dwellers do not expect,{d} and the birds will migrate away.
The Sea of Sodom{e} will cast up fish, and at night will utter a voice which many have not known, but all will hear its voice.
There will be chaos in many places, fire will break out again and again, the wild beasts will roam beyond their haunts, and women in their impurity will bring forth monsters.
Salt water will be found in the sweet, and friends one and all will attack one another. Then reason will hide itself, and understanding will withdraw into its storehouse,
and it will be sought by many and not be found; and wrong and lack of restraint will increase on earth.
One country will ask its neighbor, ‘Has righteousness, the kind that makes men just, passed through you?’ And it will say no.
In that season people will hope and not obtain; they will toil, and their ways will not prosper.
Such are the signs I am permitted to tell you. Should you pray again, and weep as now, and keep a fast of seven days, you will hear yet greater things than these.”
At that I woke; a violent shudder ran through my body, and my soul labored until it nearly gave way.
But the angel who had come and talked with me held me, gave me strength, and set me on my feet.
On the second night Salathiel,{f} the leader of the people, came to me and asked, “Where have you been? And why is your face so sad?
Are you not aware that Israel has been put in your charge in the country where they were carried away?
Rise up, then, and taste some bread, and do not abandon us, like a shepherd who leaves his flock in the power of cruel wolves.”
I told him, “Go away from me, and do not come near me for seven days, and then you may come to me.”{g} He heard what I said and left me.
So I fasted seven days, wailing and weeping, as Uriel the angel had instructed me.
After seven days{h} the thoughts of my heart were again very grievous to me,
and my soul took up once more the spirit of understanding, and I began again to speak words before the Most High.
I said, “Lord and Master, out of all the forest of the earth and all its trees you have picked one vine;
out of all the lands of the world you have picked for yourself one pit;{i} out of all the flowers of the world you have picked for yourself one lily;
out of all the depths of the sea you have filled for yourself one stream; out of all the cities ever built you have set apart Zion for yourself;
out of all the birds that were created you have named for yourself one dove; out of all the cattle that were fashioned you have chosen{j} for yourself one sheep;
and out of all the peoples that have multiplied you have gained for yourself one people; and to this people whom you desired you have granted a law approved above all.
And now, Lord, why have you handed over the one to the many, and set others above the single root,{k} and scattered your only one among many?
Those who opposed your promises have trampled on them, those who put no faith in your covenants.
If you truly hate your people, they ought to be punished by your own hands.”
When I had spoken these words, the angel who had come to me the night before was sent to me,
and said to me, “Listen to me, and I will instruct you; pay heed to me, and I will tell you more.”
“Speak, my lord,” I said. And he said to me, “You are deeply distressed in mind for Israel’s sake. Do you love him more than the One who made him?”
I said, “No, my lord, but I spoke out of grief. My heart{l} torments me every hour as I seek to grasp the path of the Most High and to search out some part of his judgment.”

He told me, “You cannot.” And I said, “Why not, lord? Why then was I born? Or why did my mother’s womb not become my grave, so that I would not have seen the travail of Jacob and the exhaustion of Israel’s race?”
He told me, “Count up for me those who have not yet come; gather for me the scattered raindrops; make the withered flowers green again for me;
open for me the chambers that are shut, and bring out for me the winds locked up in them; or show me the picture of a voice. Then I will show you the travail you ask to see.”
I said, “Lord and Master, who can know these things except one whose dwelling is not among mortals?
But I am without wisdom, so how can I speak about the things you have asked me?”
He told me, “Just as you cannot do one of the things I have named, so you will not be able to discover my judgment, or the love I have pledged to my people at the end.”
I said, “But look, lord, you are near to those who are there at the end; what then will they do who were before me, or we ourselves, or those who come after us?”
He told me, “I will liken my judgment to a ring:{m} as there is no lagging for the last, so there is no hurrying for the first.”
I replied, “Could you not have made those already made, and those now living, and those to come, all at once, so as to show your judgment the sooner?”
He replied, “The creature cannot go faster than the Creator, nor can the world hold all at once those who are to be created in it.”

I said, “How then have you told your servant that you will surely give life all at once to the creation you have made?{n} If they are indeed to live all at once, and creation will hold them, then it could hold those now present all at once.”
He told me, “Put a question to a woman’s womb: ‘If you give birth, why is it only in due time?’ Ask it, then, to deliver ten at once.”
I said, “Surely it cannot, but only each at its own time.”
He told me, “I too have made the earth a womb for those sown upon it in their own times.
For just as an infant does not bring forth, nor she who has grown old any longer,{o} so I have ordered the world I created.”
I questioned him further: “Since you have now opened the way to me, I will speak before you. Is our mother, of whom you told me, still young, or is she already nearing old age?”{p}
He replied, “Ask a woman who bears children, and she will tell you.
Say to her, ‘Why are those whom you bear now not like those you bore before, but smaller in stature?’
And she herself will answer you, ‘Those born in the prime of youth are one thing, and those born in the time of old age, when the womb is failing, are another.’
So consider for yourself as well: you people are smaller in stature than those before you,
and those who come after you will be smaller than you, as born of a creation that is already aging and passing beyond the vigor of youth.”
I said, “I beg you, lord, if I have found favor in your sight, show your servant through whom you will visit your creation.”{q}

notes.text: Latin in censu multo, “with a great census” (or “with great wealth”), apparently a corruption; the oriental versions reportedly read “with great terror.”

Latin “and the region you now see ruling will be on a set-down footprint,” an obscure phrase; the rendering follows the sense reported in the oriental versions (“a trackless waste”). The ruling country is Rome.

Latin tubam, “trumpet”; the Clementine text supplies the noun, which some manuscripts reportedly lack. The oriental versions reportedly read “after the third period” or “after the third day,” and some add that the land will be thrown into confusion.
Perhaps a reference to an unexpected ruler, or to the antichrist; the identification is uncertain.
The Dead Sea.
Latin Salathiel; other witnesses reportedly read Phaltiel (Hebrew Paltiel, “God is my deliverance”). Here the name belongs to a leader of the people, not to Ezra himself (compare 3:1 note).
The words “for seven days, and then you may come to me” are supplied from the oriental versions, as reported; the Latin ends with “do not come near me.”
The second vision runs from 5:21 to 6:34.
Latin foveam, “pit” or “hollow”; the oriental versions reportedly read “region” or “land.”
Latin providisti, “foreseen” or “provided.”
Latin “and prepared others upon the one root.”
Latin renes, “kidneys,” regarded as the seat of the emotions.
Latin coronae, “to a crown” or “wreath,” that is, a circle in which there is neither first nor last.
That is, at the resurrection. The Latin of the verse is obscure; the rendering follows the general sense.
Latin “as an infant does not bear what belongs to the old”; the rendering follows the fuller sense reported in the oriental versions.
“Our mother” is the earth (compare 10:9 and Sirach 40:1).
In the Clementine Latin, verses 55 and 56 form a single verse (5:55), so that the chapter has 55 verses; the numbering of most English versions is followed here.

verses.text: He told me, “At the start of the earthly globe, before the world’s gateways stood in place, before the gathered winds blew,
before the peals of thunder sounded, before the lightning flashes shone, before the foundations of paradise were laid,
before its lovely flowers were seen, before the powers that move were made firm,{a} before the countless hosts of angels were assembled,
before the heights of the air were lifted up, before the measures of the firmaments were named, before the furnaces in Zion were glowing hot,{b}
before the present years were searched out, before the schemes of those who now sin were estranged,{c} and before those who have stored up faith as treasure were sealed:
then I thought these things out, and they came into being through me alone and through no other; and the end shall come through me, and through no other.”
I replied, “What will divide the ages? Or when will the end of the first be, and the beginning of the one that follows?”
He told me, “From Abraham to Isaac:{d} when Jacob and Esau were born to him, Jacob’s hand gripped Esau’s heel from the start.
For Esau is the end of this world, and Jacob the beginning of the world that follows.
The hand of a man lies between heel and hand.{e} Seek nothing further, Ezra.”
I replied, “Lord and Master, if I have found grace in your eyes,
I pray you, show your servant the end of your signs, part of which you showed me on the night before.”
He replied, “Rise and stand on your feet, and you will hear a voice of the fullest sound.
There will be something like a shaking, yet the place on which you stand will not be shaken.
So when it speaks, do not take fright; for the word concerns the end, and the foundation of the earth understands.
It trembles and quakes at that speech, since it knows that at their end these things must be transformed.”
When I had heard this, I rose to my feet and listened, and there was a voice speaking, whose sound was like the roar of many waters.
It said, “Look, days are coming, and the time will be when I begin to draw near to visit the dwellers on the earth,
and when I begin to call to account those who have done harm unjustly by their wrongdoing, and when the humiliation of Zion is complete,
and when the seal is set upon the world that is about to pass away, then I will perform these signs: books will be opened before the face of the firmament, and all will see together.
Babies a year old will speak with their voices; women with child will give birth to infants before their time, at three and four months, and these will live and leap about.{f}
Sown fields will suddenly be found unsown, and full storehouses will suddenly be found empty.
A trumpet will sound aloud, and when all hear it, they will suddenly be terrified.

At that season friends will make war on friends as though they were enemies, the earth and its dwellers will be terrified, and the springs of the fountains will stand still and not run for three hours.{g}
And whoever is left of all those of whom I have told you will be saved and will see my salvation and the end of your world.
They will see those who were taken up,{h} people who have not tasted death since their birth. And the heart of earth’s dwellers will be changed and turned to another mind.
For evil will be blotted out and deceit put out like a flame;
faith will flower, corruption will be overcome, and truth will be made plain, which for so many days has been without fruit.”
While he was speaking to me, I gradually{i} gazed upon the one before whom I stood,
and he said these things to me: “I have come to show you the time of the night that is coming.{j}
If you pray once more, and fast again for seven days, I will once more tell you things greater than these, by day.{k}
For your voice has been heard before the Most High; the Mighty One has seen your upright conduct, and has taken note of the purity you have kept since your youth.
That is why he sent me to show you all this, and to tell you: Take heart, and do not fear,
and do not be quick to ponder vain things about the former times, so that you may not be hasty in the last times.”
After this I wept once more and fasted seven days in the same way, to complete the three weeks{l} I had been told of.
On the eighth night{m} my heart was troubled within me again, and I began to speak before the Most High.
For my spirit was all aflame, and my soul was in anguish.
I said, “Lord, you spoke at the beginning of creation, on the first day, saying, ‘Let heaven and earth be made,’ and your word was a finished work.
And then spirit was there, and darkness and silence hovered round about; the sound of the human voice was not yet from you.{n}
Then you commanded a shining light to be brought out of your storehouses, so that your work might be seen.
On the second day you created the spirit of the firmament and commanded it to divide and make a parting between the waters, so that one part might withdraw upward and the other remain below.

On day three you bade the waters gather into one-seventh of the earth; the other six parts you made dry and preserved, so that out of them there might be things sown by God and tilled, to serve before you.{o}
Your word went out, and straightway the deed was accomplished.
Suddenly there came forth fruit in boundless abundance, pleasures of taste of every kind, flowers of unfading color, and scents of fragrance past finding out. These were made on the third day.
On day four you bade the sun’s splendor, the moon’s light, and the array of stars come to be,
and you commanded them to serve humankind, which was about to be formed.
On the fifth day you told the seventh part, where the water had been gathered, to bring forth living creatures, birds and fish; and so it came to be.
The dumb and lifeless water produced living creatures at God’s bidding, so that from this the nations might tell of your wonders.
Then you kept two living creatures; the name of one you called Enoch,{p} and the name of the other Leviathan.{q}
You separated them from one another, for the seventh part, where the water had been gathered, could not contain them both.
To Enoch you allotted one portion, dried out on day three, as his dwelling, where a thousand mountains stand;{r}
but to Leviathan you gave the seventh part, the watery one. You have kept them to be food{s} for whom you will, and when you will.
On day six you bade the earth produce before you beasts of burden and of the field, and things that creep;
and over these Adam, whom you made ruler over all the works you had made; and from him we all come, the people you have chosen.
“All this I have told before you, Lord, because you have said that it was for our sake that you created the world.{t}
As for the other nations which have come from Adam, you have said that they are nothing, that they are like spittle, and you have likened their abundance to a drip from a jar.{u}
And now, Lord, look: these nations, which are reckoned as nothing, have begun to lord it over us and to devour us.
But we your people, whom you have called your firstborn, only begotten, your zealous one{v} and dearly loved, have been handed over into their hands.
If the world was made on our account, why is our world not ours to inherit? How much longer must this go on?”

notes.text: Latin motae virtutes, “the moving powers,” perhaps the heavenly bodies or the forces of nature.
That is, before the altar fires of the temple were kindled, or perhaps the fires of judgment (compare Isaiah 31:9).
Latin abalienarentur, “were alienated,” that is, set apart or banished; the oriental versions reportedly read “were rejected.”
Latin “From Abraham to Isaac”; the oriental versions reportedly read “From Abraham to Abraham,” that is, the dividing line runs through Abraham’s own descendants. Compare Genesis 25:26.

The Latin is obscure, reading literally “The hand of a man between the heel and the hand.” The meaning is apparently that no interval separates this age from the next, as Jacob’s hand held Esau’s heel. Other witnesses reportedly read, “For the heel of a man and the hand: between them seek nothing else.”
Latin et suscitabuntur, “and they will be raised up.” The rendering “leap about” follows the oriental versions, as reported.
Ancient clocks reckoned hours from sunrise; three hours here is simply a short span of time, not a fixed clock time.
Those taken up to heaven alive, such as Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:11); compare 14:9.
Latin paulatim, “little by little.” The oriental versions reportedly read “he looked at me,” and the Latin may be corrupt.
The meaning of this verse is uncertain; the Latin reads literally, “I have come to show you the time of the coming night.”
Latin “greater things than these by day than I have heard,” apparently corrupt.
The three weeks are the three periods of seven days’ fasting (5:13, 20; 6:31, 35).
The third vision begins here and runs to 9:25.
The meaning is that at the beginning there was as yet no voice of any human being.
Latin culta, “cultivated”; the Latin is obscure, and the rendering follows the general sense.
Latin Henoch; elsewhere, as reported, the oriental versions read Behemoth, as in Job 40:15 (Hebrew behemoth, “beasts,” a great land monster). Enoch is apparently a corruption in the Latin tradition.
Leviathan (Hebrew, perhaps “twisting one”) is the great sea monster of Job 41:1 and Isaiah 27:1. Compare 1 Enoch 60:7–9 and 2 Baruch 29:4.
Compare Psalm 50:10, where the Hebrew of “cattle on a thousand hills” uses behemoth.
Latin devorationem, “devouring”; in Jewish tradition Behemoth and Leviathan were to be food for the righteous in the messianic age (2 Baruch 29:4).
Compare Isaiah 40:15, where the nations are like a drop from a bucket.

Latin aemulatorem tuum, literally “your rival” or “one zealous for you”; the rendering “zealous one” follows the general sense. The words “and dearly loved” are supplied from the oriental versions, as reported.

verses.text: After I had ended this speech, there was sent to me the angel who had been sent on the earlier nights.
He told me, “Get up, Ezra, and listen to what I have come to say to you.”
“Speak, my God,”{a} I said. And he told me, “There is a sea set in a broad expanse, so that it is deep and vast;
but the way into it lies in a narrow place, so that it is like a river.
If someone has a mind to enter the sea, to look upon it or to be master of it, how can he reach its breadth unless he first passes through the narrows?
Here is another: a city stands built on level ground, and it is filled with every good thing.
But the way into it is narrow and set on a steep slope, with fire on the right hand and deep water on the left.
There is just one path set between them, that is, between the fire and the water, and the path has room for no more than a single footstep.
Suppose the city is granted to a man to inherit; if he never gets past the peril placed before him, how will his inheritance come to him?”
“That is so, lord,” I said. He told me, “So also is Israel’s portion.
It was for their sake that I made the world; and when Adam broke my statutes, what had been made was judged.
And so the ways into this world became narrow, grievous, and toilsome; few and evil, full of perils, and burdened with great hardship.
But the ways into the greater world are broad and safe, and they yield the fruit of immortality.
If, then, the living do not enter by these narrow and empty things, they cannot receive what has been laid up for them.
So now, why are you disturbed, since you are perishable? And why are you moved, since you are mortal?
And why have you not taken to heart what is to come, rather than what is present?”
I replied, “Lord and Master, you have laid down in your law that the righteous shall inherit these things, but that the ungodly shall perish.
The righteous, then, will endure the narrow things in hope of the broad; but those who have lived ungodly lives will have suffered the narrow things and yet will not see the broad.”
He told me, “There is no judge above God, and none who understands above the Most High.
For many now living are perishing, because the law of God that was set before them is disregarded.
For God gave strict command to those who came into the world, when they came, what they should do to live, and what they should observe to escape punishment.
But they were not persuaded; they spoke against him and devised for themselves empty thoughts;
they set before themselves the snares of sin, and declared to the Most High that he does not exist, and they did not acknowledge his ways.
His law they scorned and his promises they denied; in his statutes they put no faith, and his works they did not perform.
Therefore, Ezra, the empty receive emptiness, and the full receive fullness.
“For see, the time will come when the signs I have foretold to you will come to pass; the bride{b} will appear, the city appearing,{c} and the land now hidden will be shown.
And everyone who has been set free from the evils I have foretold will see my wonders.
For my son Jesus{d} will be revealed with those who are with him, and those who are left will rejoice four hundred years.{e}
After those years my son the Christ{f} will die, and all who have human breath.
And the world will be turned back into the ancient silence for seven days, as at the earliest judgments,{g} so that none is left.
After seven days the age that is not yet awake will be roused, and what is perishable will die.
The earth will give back those who sleep in it, and the dust those who rest there in silence; and the storehouses will give back the souls entrusted to them.
The Most High will be revealed upon the judgment seat, and miseries will pass away, and long-suffering will be withdrawn.{h}
Only judgment will remain; truth will stand, and faithfulness will grow strong.
Deeds will follow, and the reward will be shown; righteous acts will awake, and unrighteous acts will no longer rule.{i}
Then the pit{j} of torment will appear, and opposite it the place of rest; the furnace of Gehenna{k} will be displayed, and opposite it the paradise of delight.
Then the Most High will say to the nations that have been raised, ‘Look, and understand whom you have denied, whom you have not served, and whose commandments you have scorned.
Look on this side and on that: here are delight and rest, and there fire and torments.’ That is what he will say to them on the day of judgment.{l}
This is the kind of day that has no sun, no moon, no stars,
no cloud, no thunder, no lightning, no wind, no water, no air, no darkness, no evening, no morning,
no summer, no spring, no heat, no winter, no ice, no cold, no hail, no rain, no dew,
no noon, no night, no time before dawn, no gleam, no brightness, no light, but only the splendor of the glory of the Most High, by which all will begin to see what has been set before them.
For it will last as long as a week of years.{m}
This is my judgment and its ordinance; but to you alone have I shown these things.”
Then I replied, “Lord, I said it then and I say it now: Happy are those now living who keep what you have ordained!
But what of those for whom I was praying? Which of those now alive has never sinned? Or which of those ever born has not transgressed your covenant?
And now I see that the world to come will bring delight to few, but torments to many.

For an evil heart has grown up in us, which has estranged us from these things and brought us into corruption and the paths of death; it has shown us the ways of destruction and set us far off from life; and this not just a few, but nearly all who have been created.”
He replied, “Listen to me, and I will instruct you, and I will correct you once more.{n}
For this cause the Most High made two worlds, and not one.
For since you have said that the righteous are not many but few, and the ungodly abound, hear the answer to this.
If you have a very few choice stones, will you set them alongside lead and clay according to their number?{o}
I said, “Lord, how could that be?”
And he told me, “Not only that, but ask the earth, and she will tell you; flatter her, and she will relate it to you.
Say to her, ‘You produce gold and silver and copper, and also iron and lead and clay;
but silver is more plentiful than gold, and copper than silver, and iron than copper, lead than iron, and clay than lead.’
So judge for yourself which things are precious and to be desired: what is plentiful, or what is produced rarely?”
I said, “Lord and Master, what is plentiful is of less worth, for what is rarer is more precious.”
He replied, “Weigh within yourself what you have thought: whoever has what is hard to get rejoices more than one who has plenty.

So it is also with the creation I have promised;{p} for I will rejoice over the few who will be saved, because it is they who have made my glory prevail now, and through them my name has now been named.
I will not grieve over the multitude of those who perish; for they are the ones likened to vapor, made equal to flame and smoke: they caught fire, blazed up, and were quenched.”
I replied, “Earth, what is it you have given birth to, if understanding is fashioned from dust as are all other creatures?
Better had the dust itself never been born, so that the mind might not have come from it.
But as it is, the mind grows up with us, and that is why we are tormented: because we perish knowingly.
Let the human race mourn, and the wild beasts of the field be glad; let all who are born lament, but let the four-footed creatures and the cattle rejoice.
For it is far better with them than with us; they do not look for judgment, nor do they know of torments or of a salvation promised them after death.
What good is it to us that we shall be kept alive, if we are to be tormented with torment?
For all who are born are entangled in iniquities, full of sins and weighed down with offenses.
If after death we were not to come into judgment, it might perhaps have gone better with us.”
He replied, “When the Most High was making the world, and Adam and all who came after him, he first prepared the judgment and what belongs to the judgment.
Now learn from your own words, for you said that the mind grows up with us.

Those who abide on the earth will be tormented for this reason: that having understanding they did wickedness, and receiving the commandments they did not keep them, and having obtained the law they dealt falsely with what they received.
What then will they have to say at the judgment, or how will they answer in the last times?
For how long a time has the Most High shown patience toward those who inhabit the world, and not for their sake, but for the sake of the times he has foreordained!”

I replied, “If I have found grace before you, lord, show your servant this as well: after death, when each of us yields up his soul, shall we be kept at rest until those times come when you will begin to make the creation new, or are we tormented at once?”
He replied, “This too I will show you. But do not mix yourself with those who have shown scorn, and do not count yourself among those who are tormented.
A treasury of deeds is laid up for you in the Most High’s keeping, yet it will be hidden from your sight until the final times.

Now concerning death, the teaching is this: when the final sentence has gone forth from the Most High that a man shall die, as the spirit departs from the body to return again to him who gave it, it first worships the glory of the Most High.
And if the spirit belongs to the scornful, who did not walk in the Most High’s way, who held his law in contempt and loathed the God-fearing,
such spirits will not enter into dwellings, but will wander about from then on in torments, always grieving and sorrowful, in seven ways.{q}
First way: they held the Most High’s law in contempt.
The second way: because they can no longer make a good return, so as to live.
The third way: they see the reward stored up for those who have trusted the covenants of the Most High.
The fourth way: they consider the torment stored up for themselves in the last days.
The fifth way: they see the dwelling places of the others guarded by angels in deep silence.
The sixth way: they see how some of them{r} will presently pass over into torment.

The seventh way, which is greater than all those already named: they will waste away in shame and be consumed with disgrace{s} and wither with fear, as they see the glory of the Most High, before whom they sinned while alive and before whom they are to be judged in the last times.
“As for those who have kept the ways of the Most High, this is their order, when they are about to be parted from the perishable vessel.
During the time they lived in it, they served the Most High with toil and endured danger every hour, so as to keep the law of the Lawgiver perfectly.
Therefore this is the teaching concerning them:
First of all, they see with great exultation the glory of him who receives them; for they will rest in seven orders.
The first order: because they have striven with great toil to overcome the evil thought that was formed along with them, so that it should not lead them astray from life into death.
The second order: because they see the confusion in which the souls of the ungodly wander, and the punishment that awaits them.
The third order: they see the witness borne to them by him who formed them, that while they lived they kept the law entrusted to them in faith.{t}
The fourth order: they understand the rest which they now enjoy, gathered in their storehouses in deep silence, guarded by angels, and the glory that awaits them in the last days.

The fifth order: they exult because they have fled now from the perishable, and the world to come is theirs to inherit; beyond that, they behold the cramped and toilsome place from which they were freed, and the spacious one, which they are about to take up with enjoyment, deathless.
The sixth order: when it is shown to them how their face is to shine like the sun, and how they are to be made like the light of the stars, from then on incorruptible.

The seventh order, which surpasses all already named: they will exult boldly, be confident and not ashamed, and be glad and unafraid; for they hurry to look upon the face of the One they served while alive, from whose hand they are to take their wages in glory.
This is the order of the souls of the righteous, as is now announced; and the ways of torment already described are what those who have been heedless will suffer from now on.”
I replied, “Is time to be allowed, then, for the souls, once parted from their bodies, to look upon the things you have told me of?”
He said, “Their freedom will last seven days, so that they may see the things you have been told; after that they will be gathered into their dwellings.”

I replied, “If I have found grace in your eyes, show your servant this further: whether on the day of judgment the righteous will be able to plead for the ungodly or to intercede for them with the Most High,
fathers for sons, or sons for parents, brothers for brothers, kin for their nearest, or friends for those most dear to them.”

He replied, “Since you have found grace in my eyes, I will show you this as well. The day of judgment is a day of decision,{u} and it will display to all the seal of truth. For just as now a father does not send his son, or a son his father, or a master his slave, or a friend his dearest friend, to be ill in his place, or sleep, or eat, or be healed in his place,
so no one will ever ask for mercy for another on that day; for then each will bear his own unrighteousness or righteousness.”{v}
I replied,{w} “How is it, then, that we find Abraham first praying for the people of Sodom, and Moses for our ancestors who sinned in the wilderness,
and he who came after Moses{x} for Israel in the days of Achan,{y}
and Samuel{z} in the days of Saul, and David for the destruction,{aa} and Solomon for those who would come to the sanctuary,
and Elijah for those who received rain, and for one who was dead, that he might live,
and Hezekiah for the people in the days of Sennacherib, and many for many?
If, then, now that the perishable has grown great and wrong has multiplied, the just made petition for the godless, why should that not happen then too?”
He replied, “This present world is not the end, and glory does not abide in it permanently;{ab} therefore those who were strong prayed for the weak.
But the day of judgment will be the end of this age and the beginning of the age of immortality to come, in which corruption has passed away,
excess has been abolished, unbelief has been cut off, while righteousness has grown and truth has sprung up.
Then no one will be able to save one who has perished, nor to overwhelm one who has conquered.”
I replied, “This is my first word and my last: it would have been better not to give Adam the earth, or else, once it had been given, to restrain him from sinning.
For what good is it to people to live in sorrow now and to look for punishment after death?
Adam, what is this you have done? The sin was yours, yet the downfall came not on you only but on us as well, your offspring.
What good is it to us that an immortal age has been promised to us, if we have done deeds that bring death?
Or that an everlasting hope has been foretold to us, if we have become utterly worthless and vain?
Or that dwellings of health and safety are stored up for us, if we have lived wickedly?
Or that the glory of the Most High is stored up to shelter those who have lived chaste lives,{ac} if we have walked in the worst of ways?
Or that a paradise will be shown, whose fruit remains unspoiled, in which are security and healing,
if we are not to go in, since the places where we have lived were unlovely?{ad}
Or that the faces of those who practiced self-restraint will shine brighter than the stars, if our faces will be blacker than darkness?
For while we lived and did wrong, we did not consider that we would begin to suffer after death.”
He replied, “This is the meaning of the contest which every person born on the earth must wage:
if he loses, he must undergo what you have described; but if he wins, what I describe will be his.
For this is the way of which Moses spoke to the people while he was alive, saying, ‘Choose life for yourself, that you may live.’{ae}
But they did not believe him, nor the prophets after him, nor even me, who have spoken to them.
And so there will be no grief over their perdition so great as the joy over those to whom salvation is assured.”{af}
I replied, “I know, lord, that the Most High is called merciful, because he has mercy on those who have not yet come into the world;
and compassionate, because he shows compassion to those who turn back to his law;
and long-suffering, because he shows forbearance to those who have sinned, since they are his own works;
and bountiful, because he is willing to give rather than to exact;{ag}
and abounding in mercy, because he multiplies his mercies more and more to those now living, to those who are gone, and to those yet to come;
for if he did not multiply his mercies, the world would not continue with those who inhabit it;

and he grants pardon, for if he did not grant it out of his goodness, so that those who have done wickedness might be relieved of their wickedness, not one ten-thousandth of humankind could be kept alive;
and he is judge, for if he did not forgive those who were created by his word, and blot out the multitude of their offenses,{ah}
perhaps very few would be left of a countless multitude.”

notes.text: Latin Deus meus, “my God”; the oriental versions reportedly read “my lord,” as elsewhere in the book.

The bride is the heavenly Jerusalem (compare 10:25–27; Revelation 21:2). The words “the bride will appear” follow the Clementine Latin, which here is apparently corrupt; the oriental versions reportedly read “the city that is now not seen will appear.”
See the previous note.

The Latin reads “my son Jesus,” evidently a Christian alteration; the Syriac reportedly reads “my son the Messiah,” and other versions reportedly differ or omit the title. The original Jewish text spoke of the Messiah (Anointed One).

The figure of four hundred years for the messianic kingdom is found only here; the Syriac reportedly reads thirty years, and other versions reportedly differ. Compare the thousand years of Revelation 20:4–6.
Latin Christus, Greek for “Anointed One,” that is, the Messiah. The death of the Messiah before the general resurrection is a distinctive feature of this book.
Latin sicut in prioribus judiciis, “as in the former judgments”; the oriental versions reportedly read “as at the first beginnings,” that is, as before creation (compare 6:39).
Latin congregabitur, “will be gathered up,” that is, brought to an end.

Here the Clementine Latin, like the King James Version, passes directly from verse 35 to the verse numbered 106 in this translation (KJV 7:36). Verses 36–105 are the “missing fragment,” preserved in the oriental versions but lost from nearly all Latin manuscripts, because a leaf had been cut out of the ninth-century Codex Sangermanensis, from which most later Latin copies descend. Robert L. Bensly recovered the Latin text from a ninth-century manuscript at Amiens (Codex Ambianensis) and published it in 1875 as The Missing Fragment of the Latin Translation of the Fourth Book of Ezra. The removal is often thought to have been deliberate, because verse 105 denies that anyone may pray for the ungodly on the day of judgment. The translation of verses 36–105 follows Bensly’s Latin text.
Latin lacus, “pit” or “lake”; compare Revelation 20:10, 14–15.
Gehenna is the valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem (Hebrew Ge Hinnom, “valley of Hinnom”), where children were once sacrificed (Jeremiah 7:31); the name came to mean the place of final punishment.
Bensly’s Latin reads “these things you will speak, saying to them on the day of judgment”; the rendering follows the sense of the oriental versions as reported.
That is, seven years (compare Daniel 9:24–27). The oriental versions reportedly also read this.
Latin de sequenti corripiam te, “I will correct you in what follows.”

Bensly’s Latin reads “you will arrange them for yourself according to their number,” apparently a corruption; the rendering follows the sense of the oriental versions as reported. The meaning is that a few precious stones are not made worth less because they are few.
Latin repromissa creatura, “the promised creation”; the oriental versions reportedly read “the judgment that I have promised.”
The words “in seven ways” are supplied from the oriental versions, as reported; the Latin lacks them here.
Latin de eis, “of them,” that is, of the ungodly spirits.
Latin in honoribus, apparently a corruption (Bensly marks it as uncertain); the rendering follows the sense of the oriental versions as reported.
Latin per fidem, “through faith”; the phrase can also mean “in trust.” Bensly discussed both senses.
Latin dies decretorius, “the decisive day.”
Here the missing fragment ends; the next verse resumes the Clementine Latin at its 7:36.

In the Clementine Latin and the King James Version this is 7:36, and the rest of the chapter is numbered 7:36–70 there (the KJV divides it into 35 verses, as here; the Clementine into 34). In this translation it is 7:106–140, following Bensly and most modern editions. Many readers will therefore find KJV 7:36 cited as 7:106.
That is, Joshua (Joshua 7:6–9).
Latin Achaz (Ahaz), apparently a corruption of Achan (Joshua 7:1–26); the oriental versions reportedly have Achan.
The Clementine Latin reads “and Samuel,” without “in the days of Saul,” which is supplied from Bensly’s text and the oriental versions as reported. Compare 1 Samuel 7:5–9; 12:19–23.
Latin confractione, “the breaking,” that is, the plague (2 Samuel 24:15–25).
Latin “glory abides in it frequently,” apparently corrupt; the rendering follows the sense of the oriental versions as reported.
Latin qui tarde conversati sunt, “those who lived slowly,” apparently corrupt for “purely” or “chastely,” as the oriental versions reportedly read.
Latin in ingratis locis, literally “in unpleasant places.”
Deuteronomy 30:19.
Latin “to whom salvation has been persuaded,” that is, those who have been convinced of salvation.
Latin pro exigentiis, “according to demands”; the rendering follows the sense of the oriental versions as reported.
Latin “if he did not pardon those healed by his word and blot out the multitude of contentions.”

verses.text: He replied, “For the many the Most High fashioned this world; for the few, the one to come.

Let me set a likeness before you, Ezra. Put your question to the earth, and she will tell you that she supplies a great deal of soil from which clay pots are made, but only a little dust from which gold comes. So it is with the course of this present world:
numerous are those created, but those saved are few.”
I replied, “Then drink in understanding, my soul, and swallow down wisdom!{a}
For you have agreed to listen, and are eager to prophesy;{b} yet no span has been granted you except only to live.

Lord, if you do not allow your servant to pray before you, and give us seed for the heart and tilling for the understanding, so that fruit may come of it by which every mortal who bears the likeness of a human being may live,
—for you alone exist, and we are the single handiwork of your hands, as you have declared—

and just as the body is now fashioned in the womb, and you furnish its members, your creature is preserved in fire and water,{c} and for nine months the womb you fashioned bears your creature that has been created within it.
But both that which keeps and that which is kept will be kept,{d} and when the time comes the womb gives back what has grown in it.
For you have commanded that from the very members, that is, from the breasts, milk be supplied to the fruit of the breasts,
so that what was fashioned may be nourished for a time; and afterward you will guide it in your mercy.
You reared it in your righteousness, instructed it in your law, and corrected it by your understanding.
You will put it to death as your creation, and make it live as your work.
If, then, you destroy with a light command one who was fashioned with such great labor, to what purpose was he made?{e}
And now I will speak: about humankind as a whole you know best; but I will speak about your people, for whose sake I am grieved,
and about your inheritance, for whom I mourn, and about Israel, for whom I am sad, and about Jacob, for whom I am in pain.
Therefore I will begin to pray before you for myself and for them, for I see the failings of us who inhabit the earth;
but I have heard how swiftly the judgment will come.{f}
So hear my voice and understand my speech, and I will speak before you.”
The beginning of the words of Ezra’s prayer, before he was taken up.{g} He said: “Lord, you who abide for ever,{h} whose eyes are lifted up to the heights and the air,
whose throne is beyond estimating and whose glory is beyond grasping, before whom the host of angels stands trembling,
whose service takes the form of wind and fire,{i} whose word is true and whose sayings endure,
whose command is mighty and whose ordinance is terrible, whose look dries up the deeps and whose anger makes the mountains melt away, and whose truth bears witness:{j}
give ear to the prayer of your servant, and attend to the petition of your creature.
While I live I will speak, and while I have understanding I will answer.
Do not regard the sins of your people, but those who serve you faithfully.
Pay no heed to the godless pursuits of the nations, but to those who have kept your testimonies through sufferings.
Do not think of those who have lived deceitfully before you, but call to mind those who have known your fear according to your will.
Do not resolve to destroy those who have behaved like cattle, but look upon those who have taught your law with splendor.
Do not be indignant with those judged worse than beasts, but love those who have always trusted in your righteousness and glory.
For we and our fathers languish in such maladies; but because of us sinners you will be called merciful.
For if you are pleased to have mercy on us, who have no works of righteousness, then you will be called merciful.
For the righteous, who have many works stored up with you, will receive their reward from their own deeds.
But what is man, that you should be angry with him? Or what is a perishable race, that you should be so bitter toward it?
Truly, of all ever born there is none who has not behaved godlessly, and of those who confess you{k} there is none who has not gone astray.
For in this, Lord, your righteousness and your goodness will be made known, when you show mercy to those who have no store of good works.”
He replied, “Some things you have spoken rightly, and it will turn out according to your words.
For truly I will not concern myself with the fashioning of those who have sinned, or with their death, their judgment, or their destruction;
but I will rejoice over the creation of the righteous, and remember also their pilgrimage, their salvation, and the reward they will receive.
As I have spoken, therefore, so it is.
